replies.text:
Checklist against commonly-missed threats:

- Automated abuse (brute force, flooding, mass sign-up, scraping): design has no sign-in, form or API endpoint described — only "the app accepts any TLS certificate when the environment flag is set" — not applicable.
- Staff/admin screens showing user-supplied content: nothing in the design mentions any screen or content submission — not applicable.
- Unlogged privileged actions (delete, refund, role change, money): no such action described; the only state change is a config flag — the related accountability angle is not covered by the list but is weaker than the gaps below.
- Cacheable personal/financial documents: no documents or pages described — not applicable.
- Attacker-controlled text reaching logs/CSV/email/headers: design names no logging or export path — not applicable.
- Confidentiality of traffic once validation is bypassed ("accepts any TLS certificate"), with signal `secretHandling: true`: listed threats cover impersonation and response tampering only — **not covered**.
- Flag shipped enabled by whoever builds the release ("read from a config file bundled in the release build"): listed threats cover an attacker unpacking/repackaging a build, not an insider enabling it fleet-wide — **not covered**.

{
  "schema": "threatline.threatmodel.v1",
  "issueKey": "EVAL-07",
  "sketch": {
    "components": ["mobile app", "TLS client", "bundled release config file", "environment flag", "backend API"],
    "dataStores": ["bundled config file in release build"],
    "externalServices": ["backend API over TLS"],
    "trustBoundaries": ["device to backend network link", "release build pipeline to production installs"],
    "dataClasses": ["credentials", "secrets"],
    "exposure": "internal",
    "llmFeatures": false
  },
  "threats": [
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "Credentials and secrets in app traffic are readable once any certificate is accepted",
      "scenario": "An attacker running a transparent proxy on shared Wi-Fi or an upstream network sees the full plaintext of every request and response from an install where the flag is set, because the app accepts any TLS certificate. Unlike impersonating the backend, the goal here is harvesting: login credentials, session tokens and API keys the app sends to the backend. The attacker then replays those secrets directly against the backend from their own machine, outliving the network position.",
      "component": "Mobile app TLS client / backend API traffic",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 5,
      "rating": { "attacker": "anyone", "effort": "low", "reach": "many", "harm": "sensitive_data" },
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "To help testing, the app accepts any TLS certificate when the environment flag is set." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V9.2.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-295", "CWE-319"],
      "plainLanguage": "With certificate checks off, anyone on the network can read the app's traffic in the clear and steal the passwords and tokens it sends.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Credentials must never traverse a connection with unverified certificates",
        "given": "an app build that can accept any TLS certificate",
        "when": "the app is about to send credentials, session tokens or API keys",
        "then": "the request must be refused unless the server certificate chain and hostname were validated, so secrets are never exposed in plaintext to a proxy"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "ElevationOfPrivilege",
      "title": "Whoever controls the release config can ship accept-any-certificate to the entire production fleet",
      "scenario": "The flag lives in a config file bundled in the release build, so it is set by the build/release process, not by the device owner. An insider with build or config access (or anyone who compromises the pipeline) sets the flag in one release and every production install downgrades to accepting any certificate at once. No user action or device compromise is needed, and the testing-only trust model becomes the shipped default for all users.",
      "component": "Release build pipeline / bundled config file",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 5,
      "rating": { "attacker": "insider", "effort": "low", "reach": "all", "harm": "integrity" },
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "The flag is read from a config file bundled in the release build." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V14.2.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-489", "CWE-1188"],
      "plainLanguage": "Because the switch is set when the app is built, one release change can turn off certificate checking for every user at once.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Certificate bypass must be impossible in release builds",
        "given": "a build targeting production distribution",
        "when": "the environment flag requesting certificate bypass is present in the bundled config",
        "then": "the bypass code must be absent from the release binary (compiled out for non-debug builds) and the build must fail rather than ship a fleet-wide bypass"
      }
    }
  ]
}
